A database index works like the index at the back of a book. Instead of reading every page to find a topic, you look it up in the index and go straight to the relevant pages. A database can similarly use an index to find matching rows without checking the whole table.

For example, an index on a customer table’s email column can help the database quickly find the customer with a particular email address.

The tradeoff is that indexes take up storage and need upkeep. When relevant data is inserted, updated, or deleted, the database must update the index too, adding work to those writes. An index can speed up reads, but not every query benefits. Its usefulness depends on what the query needs to find.

The new page had more signups because it received twice as many visitors, but a smaller share signed up: 160 out of 2,000 visitors, or 8%, compared with 100 out of 1,000, or 10%, for the old page.

The observed conversion rate is therefore lower for the new page. These are descriptive results; without a significance analysis, we haven’t established whether the difference reflects more than chance variation.

We don’t yet know whether the reminder emails reduced missed appointments. The rate fell from 18% in August to 12% in September, when the emails began. But September also had a different mix of appointment types and a new cancellation policy, which could have contributed to the decline.

Without a randomized comparison, the data shows an association, not a demonstrated causal effect. Next, compare the same appointment types across the two months and, if feasible, test reminders using randomized assignment to better isolate their effect.

Daily visitors are counted once each day they visit. Weekly visitors are counted once across the whole week. Someone visiting Monday and Tuesday adds one to each day’s count but only one to the weekly count, so adding the daily numbers can give a higher total.

This is expected behavior, not a reporting error. We should label the views “daily unique visitors” and “weekly unique visitors” to make the distinction clearer.
